outline.description: Sets the stage for the dispute, the patents, accused technology, jury verdict, post-trial motions, standards of review, and the Federal Circuit’s scope of review.
subtopics: Parties and accused technology: AT&T’s use of Nokia radios with PIM-C feature; Nokia’s intervention
Asserted patents and claims: ’134 patent (claims 1–3) and ’775 patent (claims 1, 4, 9, 16, 21, 29, 36)
Jury verdict: validity, infringement on all asserted claims, and $166.3M lump-sum damages
Post-trial: JMOL of noninfringement and damages; motion for new trial on damages; district court denials
Appellate jurisdiction: 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)

Standards of review: Fifth Circuit de novo review of JMOL denials; substantial-evidence review of jury infringement findings; de novo claim construction with clear-error review for subsidiary factual findings; abuse-of-discretion for new-trial denials

outline.chapter_title: Technical and Claim Frame: IMP/PIM Mitigation and the Accused Architecture
outline.description: Explains the radio-interference concepts and the relevant claim structures to contextualize the infringement analyses.
subtopics: IMP and PIM concepts: multiple transmit signals combining at obstacles to form in-band interference; internal vs. external PIM

’134 patent overview: receiver-side method—oversampling a passband containing both signals of interest and interference-generating signals; decimation, IMP estimation, cancellation; closed-loop phase/amplitude adjustment with sub-sample phase shifts

’775 patent overview: receiver-side cancellation using three signals S1, S2, S3; seven specified third-order digital multiplications based on a power-series nonlinearity model; passive IMPs generated after HPA and transmitter filter
Key accused components/processes from Nokia materials: RF ADC sampling, GROOT FPGA PIM model, DL(TX) reference, modeled PIM path, signals x1, x2, use of complex conjugates and moduli

outline.chapter_title: ’134 Patent: Why Substantial Evidence Was Lacking
outline.description: Analyzes the failure of proof on the ’134 patent’s oversampling limitation that requires sampling a passband containing both the signals of interest and the interference-generating signals.
subtopics: Disputed limitation: Claim 1[a] requires the receiver to oversample a passband of received signals containing both signals of interest and interference-generating signals
Finesse’s mapping at trial: Dr. Wells identified DL(TX) reference as the signal of interest and modeled PIM path as the interference-generating signals, both allegedly on the red path into the RF ADC
Temporal impossibility critique: modeled PIM path is generated downstream in the GROOT FPGA after ADC sampling; cannot be sampled before it is generated

Cross-examination pivot: references to x1 and x2 as two inputs, but no clear mapping of x1/x2 to the claim-required categories; continued assertions that the modeled PIM path was the interference-generating signals
District court’s JMOL denial rationale: inferred that Dr. Wells actually meant x1 and x2; treated the modeled PIM path as not the interference-generating signals

Appellate holding: testimony was confusing and self-contradictory; no clear mapping tying x1/x2 to claimed categories; reliance on contradictory expert testimony cannot constitute substantial evidence (Johns Hopkins v. Datascope); reversal of JMOL denial for noninfringement

outline.chapter_title: ’775 Patent: Three Signals and Seven Multiplications
outline.description: Dissects the claim-construction dispute, prosecution history arguments, and evidentiary shortcomings regarding the seven required multiplications.
subtopics: Key limitations: use of three signals S1, S2, S3 (separately identifiable) and generation of an n-th order ICS via seven specific third-order multiplications
Claim construction: district court construed S1, S2, S3 as separately identifiable but not necessarily unique; inventor testimony supported that they can be same or different

Prosecution history argument: Appellants’ claim-scope surrender theory based on amendment from “two or three signals” to “three signals”; Federal Circuit rejects clear and unambiguous disavowal—amendment does not bar systems with two unique inputs so long as three separately identifiable signals are used
Evidence of the multiplications: Nokia document shows only three distinct forms (x1·|x1|·|x1|, x1·x1·x2', x1·|x2|·|x2|) with modulus and complex conjugate operations

Mapping failure: Dr. Wells did not show how the accused operations correspond to all seven claimed multiplications; appellate attempt to map was not presented to the jury and relied on signals vs. their conjugates/moduli inconsistently
Ten-multiplication argument: record did not identify which subset maps to the seven claimed; absence of concrete mapping means no substantial evidence
Result: reversal of JMOL denial for noninfringement of all asserted ’775 claims due to failure of proof on the seven-multiplication requirement

outline.description: Explains the consequence of the noninfringement rulings for damages and the ultimate judgment.
subtopics: Damages posture: $166.3M lump-sum award; JMOL and new-trial motions denied below
Standard of review for new trial: abuse of discretion (Fifth Circuit)
Effect of noninfringement: with JMOL reversals on both patents, the Federal Circuit vacates the damages award
Final judgment: reversed (noninfringement JMOL denials) and vacated (damages); costs to defendants-appellants
